For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).
</problem>

### 1. A consequence of the stated Oka property

If \(Y\) is Oka, every continuous plurisubharmonic function \(u:Y\to\mathbb R\) bounded above is constant on each connected component.

Indeed, let \(f\) be any small affine holomorphic disc whose closed image lies in \(Y\). The stated approximation property gives entire maps \(F_j:\mathbb C\to Y\) converging uniformly to \(f\) on that disc. Each \(u\circ F_j\) is bounded-above subharmonic on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant. Continuity of \(u\) shows that \(u\circ f\) is constant. Applying this to all sufficiently small affine discs proves local constancy, and therefore constancy on components.

### 2. A smooth Oka domain has no strictly pseudoconvex boundary point

Suppose that \(q\) were such a point of a domain \(Y\). A local defining function \(r\), with \(Y=\{r<0\}\), can be replaced by \(r+Ar^2\) so that its full complex Hessian at \(q\) is positive definite. Its Taylor expansion then gives a holomorphic polynomial \(P\), with \(P(q)=0\), and constants \(c,R>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{Re}P(z)\le -c\|z-q\|^2
\qquad(z\in Y\cap B(q,R)).
\]
Choose \(0<\delta<cR^2/4\). Define
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\operatorname{Re}P(z)+\delta,0\},
   &z\in Y\cap B(q,R),\\
0,&z\in Y\setminus B(q,R).
\end{cases}
\]
The two definitions agree on an interior neighbourhood of the artificial spherical boundary: whenever \(R/2\le\|z-q\|<R\), the maximum is zero. Consequently \(u\) is continuous and plurisubharmonic on \(Y\), with \(0\le u\le\delta\). It is positive at points approaching \(q\), but zero away from that small neighbourhood. Taking \(R\) sufficiently small makes it nonconstant on the relevant component. This contradicts Step 1.

### 3. Application in complex dimension two

Let \(K\in\mathcal K_2\), and suppose \(\mathbb C^2\setminus K\) is Oka. If \(\partial K\) were not pseudoconvex, its Levi form would be negative on its one-dimensional complex tangent space at some point. The complementary defining function \(-\rho\) would therefore be strictly pseudoconvex there, contradicting Step 2. Thus
\[
\boxed{2\in N}.
\]
